name: Cultural Nationalism
summary: Cultural nationalism defines the nation by a shared language, history and way of life and aims to preserve, revive and develop that culture, chiefly through intellectual, educational and artistic work. It does not require a separate state: the cultural nation may be protected through autonomous institutions within a larger polity. Its main thinkers stress language as the carrier of a people's memory and spirit, and it has no economic programme of its own.
scope: The classic cultural-nationalist tradition from Herder and Fichte through Hutchinson's account of cultural nationalists as moral innovators, with moderate cultural strands such as the Hindutva self-description and liberal cultural nationalism as discussed by Gans and Tamir. It excludes ethnic or racial nationalism, economic nationalism and the state-building programmes of political nationalism. Most social, economic and institutional statements are outside the doctrine and are answered 0 with low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Johann Gottfried Herder
keyFigures.role: Philosopher who defined the nation by language and culture and prized cultural diversity.

keyFigures.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
keyFigures.role: Philosopher whose Addresses to the German Nation tied national spirit to language and education.

sources.usedFor: Language as the basis of national identity, education of the young, the state as secondary to the nation.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Cultural nationalism concerns shared culture and identity; none of the sources treat health policy, so adherents divide along ordinary left-right lines.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy is outside a doctrine about cultural community, and the sources give no position, so adherents split by their wider economics.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Cultural nationalism has no economic programme in the sources used; Fichte even subordinates the state to the nation rather than to markets.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the cultural-nationalist sources addresses ownership of utilities; adherents range from market liberals to state-minded nationalists.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Taxation of wealth is not a cultural-nationalist question and the sources are silent, so no side is inferable.

unions-good.rationale: The doctrine is about cultural community, not labour organisation; no source states a position on unions.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property rights are not addressed by cultural nationalism in the sources; adherents are split between conservative and left variants.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporate regulation is not discussed in the sources on cultural nationalism, so this is left neutral.

cut-welfare.rationale: Cultural nationalism does not address welfare design; this cannot be inferred from its stress on cultural community.

worker-ownership.rationale: Worker ownership is an economic-structure question that the cultural-nationalist sources never raise.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Security-versus-liberty trade-offs are not part of the doctrine; Fichte values freedom as the soil of culture but says nothing on surveillance.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy is not addressed by cultural nationalism; adherents vary with their wider conservatism or liberalism.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The sources do not address speech regulation; cultural nationalists include liberal and conservative strands that would differ.

strong-leader.rationale: Herder wanted loosely federated, republican, minimally coercive government and Fichte said the state is not an end in itself, which weighs against rule by a gridlock-bypassing leader.

state-harmful.rationale: Cultural nationalists want institutions that sustain and protect the culture, and Fichte holds the state serves the nation's development, so abolishing the state is not their aim.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun control is not addressed by the doctrine and adherents split along wider cultural-political lines.

empower-police-military.rationale: Policing and military funding are not cultural-nationalist questions; Herder was hostile to militarism but others in the family are not.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Sexual morality policy is not part of cultural nationalism and adherents differ across strands.

decide-locally.rationale: Herder favoured loose federation and local government, but Fichte and statist strands favour national institutions, so the family is split.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal philosophy is not addressed by the cultural-nationalist sources.

traditional-family.rationale: Cultural nationalists value inherited tradition, but the sources make no claim about family forms and modernising strands differ.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; cultural nationalists include both tradition-minded and liberal adherents.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed in the sources on cultural nationalism; adherents split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Cultural nationalists often count religion as part of national culture (Hindutva), but Herder interpreted sacred texts by secular means and the family is split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Racial-redress policy is not addressed by the sources; Herder rejected race as a category but gave no policy view.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not addressed by cultural nationalism; adherents differ with their wider outlook.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Preserving and sustaining the culture across generations is the defining aim; Gans, cited in the SEP, says a people has a morally significant interest in sustaining its culture, and Hutchinson describes cultural nationalists as renewing national identity.

gradual-change.rationale: Cultural nationalists revive and reinvent heritage, which is neither plainly gradualist nor radical; Hutchinson calls them moral innovators in crises.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Immigration is not addressed directly in the SEP, but a movement centred on a shared culture tends to favour limits that protect it; liberal strands would resist.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Not discussed directly; a focus on the nation's cultural self-determination suggests reluctance to cede authority, though Herder's cosmopolitanism softens this.

free-trade.rationale: Trade policy is not addressed by cultural nationalism and the sources give no position.

nation-first.rationale: Fichte puts nation above all, but Herder ranked humankind above fatherland and rejected a favourite people, so the family is split.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Not addressed; Herder condemned imperial war but the doctrine has no stance on intervention.

open-borders.rationale: Open borders would erode the culturally defined nation, which is the unit a cultural nationalist seeks to sustain; the SEP notes the tension between difference and shared national identity.

limit-growth.rationale: Environmental limits are not addressed in the sources.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed by cultural nationalism; adherents differ with wider politics.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The sources do not address technological optimism.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy is outside the doctrine.

revolution-justified.rationale: Cultural nationalists often act as intellectual renewers rather than revolutionaries, but the sources do not rule out revolt; the family is mixed.

experts-over-public.rationale: Not addressed; Hutchinson stresses intellectuals as shapers of national identity, but that is not technocracy.

central-planning.rationale: Economic planning is not addressed by the sources.

land-value-tax.rationale: Tax design is not addressed by the doctrine.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance tax is outside the doctrine and the sources are silent.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Economic nationalism is a separate strand; cultural nationalism as described in the sources concerns culture, so no position is inferable.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial policy is not addressed in the sources.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Property distribution is not addressed by the doctrine.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not discussed; cultural nationalists seek to preserve inherited national life and rarely propose abolishing the monetary economy.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; some organic-nationalist strands favour it but cultural nationalism as such does not.

one-party-rule.rationale: Herder favoured republican, participatory government and Fichte did not tie the nation to a party; the sources give no support for single-party rule.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Not addressed; cultural nationalists have lived under monarchies and republics alike.

democracy-best.rationale: Herder favoured republicanism and broad participation, but other strands, including Fichte, were less committed to democracy as such.

workers-councils.rationale: Not discussed; a doctrine built on a nation-wide cultural community does not rest on class councils.

right-to-secede.rationale: Self-determination is central, but the SEP notes a cultural nation need not have its own state and secession is contested; adherents split.

natural-rulers.rationale: Herder opposed autocracy and the notion of favoured peoples; the sources do not support natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: Herder condemned war but the sources give no general rule, and political nationalists drawn from cultural movements have used force.

war-builds-character.rationale: Herder condemned military conflict as serving rulers at the people's expense; cultural nationalism as a culture-building movement does not celebrate war.

separate-church-state.rationale: Religion is part of national culture for some (Hindutva) and not others; the family is split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Cultural nationalism typically treats religion as culture rather than law; the RSS describes Hindu as a cultural, not religious, concept.

military-superiority.rationale: Cultural nationalism as such does not address military posture; Herder opposed militarism.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Herder defined the nation by language and culture rather than race, and cultural nationalists contrast themselves with ethnic definitions, though cultural nations often share descent in practice.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Cultural nationalism sees history as driven by peoples, their cultures and ideas rather than by class conflict.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed directly; the SEP notes that cultural groups may claim devolved authority in their homelands, which suggests some sympathy but not a stated position.

civilizational-union.rationale: Herder welcomed exchange among peoples, but cultural nationalism is organised around particular nations rather than blocs, so this is unclear.

self-interest-moral.rationale: A movement oriented to communal culture and duty to the nation is unlikely to endorse self-interest as the moral basis, though it is not stated.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Fichte subordinates the individual to national development, while Herder and liberal nationalists stress individual and human rights; split.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Nature's intrinsic value is an environmental-ethics question that the cultural-nationalist sources never take up; no side is inferable.

limit-population.rationale: Population control is not a topic in the cultural-nationalism literature, so nothing supports either side.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Some Romantic cultural nationalists lamented modernity, but the sources do not take this as the doctrine's position.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Speeding up technological change is not discussed in the sources, and cultural nationalists include both modernisers and preservers.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bodily enhancement is outside the doctrine's concerns with language, history and national identity.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Not discussed; a doctrine rooted in historically formed national character is unlikely to hand governance to algorithms.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption policy is a modern security question the cultural-nationalist sources do not touch.

restore-past-order.rationale: Cultural nationalists revive a heritage but, per Hutchinson, as moral innovators who offer a new map of identity, so restoration versus progress is split.

direct-action.rationale: Not addressed; cultural nationalists work mainly through cultural societies, schools and the arts.

means-match-ends.rationale: The sources say nothing about whether methods must mirror aims, which is a debate of revolutionary and anarchist movements.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Cultural nationalism builds national communities around literate culture, language and historical memory, which is incompatible with abandoning civilisation.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Abolishing the division of labour is a Marxist and utopian idea with no counterpart in cultural-nationalist writing.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distribution by need is a communist principle the cultural-nationalist sources neither endorse nor reject.

production-for-use.rationale: Production for use versus profit is an economic-system question the doctrine does not address.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Cultural nationalism does not hold a labour theory of exploitation; the sources treat identity, not class.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: A doctrine that places the nation and its culture above class holds no brief for class dictatorship.

collective-farming.rationale: Farm organisation is outside a doctrine about national culture, though romantic strands idealise peasants without prescribing collectivisation.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not addressed; Herder blamed autocratic rulers for war rather than an economic system.

taxation-theft.rationale: Cultural nationalists seek institutions to sustain culture, which need public funding; the sources do not discuss tax.

harm-principle.rationale: Not addressed; Fichte values freedom but ties it to national education.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The SEP presents cultural nationalism as granting a group a morally significant interest in sustaining its culture, which is a collective claim.

conscription.rationale: Not addressed; Fichte stressed national education but the doctrine takes no stated view on military service.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The relative weight of exit and voting is a libertarian debate that cultural nationalism does not address.

state-as-business.rationale: Fichte insists the state is not an end in itself and exists for the nation's development, which sits poorly with treating citizens as customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Cultural nationalists stress cultural belonging; the sources give no view on freedom as material capacity.

media-academia-power.rationale: Hutchinson stresses intellectuals' formative role, but the sources do not claim they outrank elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Herder rejected the concept of race and defined nations by language and culture, so a cultural nationalist does not ground difference in genetics.

organic-representation.rationale: Not addressed; some organic nationalists favour it but cultural nationalism as such does not.

total-state.rationale: Herder wanted minimal coercion and loose federation, and Fichte calls the state secondary to the nation; Hutchinson treats culture-building as civil-society work.

national-rebirth.rationale: Hutchinson describes cultural nationalists as moral innovators in times of crisis who renew the national community with historical myths, though not necessarily in a radical sense.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Herder strongly opposed imperialism and colonialism, and cultural nationalism seeks cultural flourishing rather than conquest, though political offshoots vary.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: A modern doctrine of national culture does not rest authority on feudal oaths; the sources are silent.

bound-labor.rationale: Serfdom is incompatible with the shared, free national culture cultural nationalists seek; Fichte calls freedom the soil of culture.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Herder stressed that concepts vary by culture and period, which gives partial support, but the sources do not claim knowledge is only power.

universal-morality.rationale: Herder stressed deep value differences between cultures yet affirmed equal moral respect; the family leans particularist.

single-common-good.rationale: Not addressed directly; Herder's pluralism cuts against it and Fichte's organic nation leans toward it.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Cultural Zionism is cited in the cultural-nationalism literature and the SEP allows a cultural nation to have a state, but the sources do not state a position on Israel.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; shared-culture logic could support it but the sources give no position.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language is central: Herder treated it as the core of a people's memory and spirit, and Fichte treats the national language as the basis of the nation, so reviving one is a characteristic cultural-nationalist project.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Company governance is not covered by the cultural-nationalist sources.

school-vouchers.rationale: Cultural nationalists care what schools teach (Fichte on national education) but not how schools are funded, so no side follows.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy is outside the doctrine and the sources give no view.

economic-freedom.rationale: Not addressed; Fichte ties freedom to culture generally, not markets.

rule-by-example.rationale: Herder favoured moral formation through exemplary individuals, but the sources do not extend this to government.

national-self-determination.rationale: Self-determination is central to nationhood in the SEP, but for cultural nationalists it may be met by autonomy within a multinational federation and not necessarily a separate state.

force-without-un.rationale: Authorisation for force abroad is a question of international law the doctrine does not take up.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Cultural nationalism is a Romantic movement grounded in myth, memory and feeling about the nation; Hutchinson stresses historical myths as the tool.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Not addressed; a shared-culture view might favour it but the sources are silent.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Welfare conditionality is not addressed by the cultural-nationalism sources.

class-collaboration.rationale: Cultural nationalism treats the nation as a unified community above class, which suggests cooperation, though the sources do not state it.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Cultural nationalism exists to preserve inherited heritage, and the studies cited describe its use of history, libraries and museums to sustain national identity.

workers-nation.rationale: Cultural nationalists frame solidarity in national terms, though the sources do not discuss labour organisation.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury bans belong to religious and economic traditions, not to cultural nationalism as described.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Herder rejected race and cultural nationalism defines the nation by culture, so legal racial separation is not part of it.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Cultural nationalism does not analyse the state as a class tool; Fichte sees it as an instrument of national development.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy production is not addressed by the doctrine.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: A culturally defined nation expects newcomers to join its culture, though the SEP records liberal nationalists who want identity to stay dynamic and absorb new elements.

elite-replacement.rationale: The conspiracy claim is a feature of ethnic and far-right nationalism, not cultural nationalism as described in the sources.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral-system design is not part of the cultural-nationalist programme in the sources.

national-mission.rationale: Herder rejected favourite peoples and imperialism, and cultural nationalism seeks to cultivate its own culture rather than export a political form, though Fichte gave Germans a special role.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Structural analyses of gender power are not addressed in the cultural-nationalist sources.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Anti-elite claims belong to populism; the sources on cultural nationalism, which stress intellectuals' role, do not make this charge.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics is not part of the cultural nationalism described in the sources, which rejects biological definitions of the nation.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Transitional-justice questions are not addressed by the sources.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Cultural nationalists want institutions that protect and develop the culture, so a minimal state that ignores culture is not their programme.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Herder rejected race and cultural nationalism defines membership by culture, which makes discouraging racial mixing foreign to it.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Herder held equal moral respect for all people and grounded it partly in their diversity; other strands are less explicit.

socialism-one-country.rationale: This is an internal debate of Marxism-Leninism with no bearing on cultural nationalism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Cultural nationalism as described takes no stated view on how to classify settler states, though Herder opposed colonialism in general.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: In India the Hindutva strand favours it, but cultural nationalism in general does not address it.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Hindutva-linked cultural nationalists support restrictions while other strands do not; split.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A Hindutva-specific position; other cultural nationalisms are silent, so no general stance.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Not addressed; depends on whether the national culture includes a religion.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Socialist-state doctrine is outside the topic.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Herder favoured republican participation, but Fichte grounded the state in the nation's development, so adherents differ.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade aims belong to economic nationalism, not to the cultural variety, which says nothing of export targets.

population-transfer.rationale: Herder's respect for every nation and the SEP's emphasis on inclusive identity cut against expelling minorities, which belongs to ethnic nationalism.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The non-aggression principle is a libertarian doctrine and no cultural-nationalist source takes it up.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Herder stressed peaceful cooperation and exchange between peoples and condemned war.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Party bans are not discussed in the sources, and adherents' stance depends on their wider liberal or authoritarian leanings.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Not addressed, though Herder opposed domination of one culture by another.

separated-powers.rationale: Constitutional design is not addressed by the doctrine, which concerns national culture rather than institutions' structure.

vanguard-party.rationale: Cultural nationalists see the intelligentsia as shaping national identity but not as a disciplined class vanguard.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Priority to the poor is not part of a doctrine about cultural community.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing tenure policy is outside the doctrine.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Labour law is not addressed by cultural nationalism.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusian explanations of poverty are not part of the cultural-nationalist sources.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The doctrine rests on a shared culture as the basis of the community, and the SEP discusses the tension, but Herder valued diversity between nations and liberal strands disagree.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not discussed; a doctrine of national character formed by elites and education is unlikely to favour lottery.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Emergency powers are not addressed in the cultural-nationalist sources.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls are an economic-policy matter the doctrine does not address.

party-controls-media.rationale: Herder and the SEP's liberal strand favour open cultural exchange, and cultural nationalism works through civil society, though state strands differ.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not discussed; party control of the army belongs to revolutionary-party ideologies, not cultural nationalism.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: A culturally defined nation tends to expect immersion before membership, but the sources do not discuss naturalisation periods.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay rules for representatives are a radical-democratic concern absent from the sources.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline is a question of party organisation, not of cultural nationalism, which works largely through cultural societies.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The SEP says nation and state are loosely linked and a nation could live in a federation, which gives some openness, but no stance on the EU is stated.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Command of the armed forces is a constitutional detail the doctrine does not specify.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is a theological and institutional question with no cultural-nationalist position.

clerical-rule.rationale: Cultural nationalism treats religion as one element of culture and Herder read sacred texts by secular means, so clerical rule is not implied.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Cultural nationalists identify with their nation, so working for its defeat is opposed to the doctrine; this is a Leninist position.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Fichte and Herder valued art and literature for forming national character, but neither is documented as favouring censorship.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Presidential term rules are not addressed by the doctrine.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of officials is not in the cultural-nationalist sources.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy is not addressed; the sources concern culture rather than foreign-policy posture.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Housing tenure is far from the concerns of cultural nationalism.

people-in-arms.rationale: Militia versus professional army is not covered by the cultural-nationalism sources.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: A shared culture across a border supports union of the nation, though the SEP notes the nation need not have a single state.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Romantic cultural nationalists often idealised the peasantry as the keeper of folk culture, but the sources do not state it as doctrine.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Cultural nationalism is largely an intellectual movement, so it does not scorn the educated; populist strands might.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Herder held that cultures differ and none is a favourite, but Fichte and other strands ranked their own nation highly, so agreement is moderate.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment is not addressed by the doctrine; adherents differ with their wider politics.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Cultural nationalists care about schooling for national identity, but the sources give no view on sex education.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Curriculum disputes over evolution are not part of cultural nationalism as described.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Obscenity law is not addressed in the sources.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Cultural nationalism defines nationhood by culture, which can be acquired, so it does not require descent, but heritage-minded strands differ.

minority-language-support.rationale: Herder held that every nation should be respected and advanced, and the SEP lists cultural institutions and devolution to protect minority cultures, though the nation's own language is primary.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Exemptions for religious minorities are not discussed in the cultural-nationalism sources.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Cultural nationalists seek a shared culture and sometimes cultural homogenisation, per the Wikipedia article, so conformity is valued more.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Third-world debt is not addressed by the doctrine.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Cultural nationalism stresses cultural rather than economic transformation, but the sources do not take up this claim about independence.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Procedures for rewriting constitutions are not addressed by the sources.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Development-dictatorship arguments are not part of the cultural-nationalist sources; Fichte even calls freedom the soil of culture.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Herder's cosmopolitanism points toward concern for all humanity, but no position on aid is stated.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear strategy is outside the doctrine.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Method of electing the head of state is not addressed in the sources.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central-bank design is not addressed by cultural nationalism.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Not addressed directly; attachment to a cultural homeland suggests some support but the sources do not state it.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Social-function theories of property are not addressed by the cultural-nationalist sources.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A debate within Marxism about the USSR that cultural nationalism does not take up.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk rules are outside the doctrine.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliance guarantees such as NATO's are not addressed by the cultural-nationalism sources.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Not addressed, though national self-determination is a central value in the SEP.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Church-state power balance depends on whether religion is part of the national culture, which the sources leave open.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The ceremonial role of a head of state is not addressed, though a symbol of unity would suit a cultural community.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The doctrine does not require statehood and the SEP notes states often resist secession, but no position follows.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The SEP discusses autonomy for cultural nations within larger states, but this economic-legal arrangement is not stated.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Herder was republican and anti-autocratic and Fichte makes the state secondary to the nation, so a sacred ruler has no place.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Income-tax structure is not addressed by the doctrine.

character-from-environment.rationale: Herder and cultural nationalists stress that language, history and upbringing shape a people's character rather than race, though the sources do not state this for individuals.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Herder favoured republican limits on rulers and no source supports an unbound sovereign.

space-expansion.rationale: Space as a civilisational goal is not part of the sources on cultural nationalism.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-constitution theory is not part of the cultural-nationalist sources.

leader-cult.rationale: Cultural nationalism centres the national culture rather than a leader, and Herder opposed autocracy.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody law is not addressed by the doctrine.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist doctrine about socialist societies that cultural nationalism does not address.

land-redistribution.rationale: Agrarian reform is not addressed in the cultural-nationalist sources.

refugee-return.rationale: Return of refugees is not addressed, though shared-culture logic might sympathise with a displaced people.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Cultural nationalism as described stresses cultural protection and self-determination, which may be met without a state, rather than irredentism, though political offshoots differ.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Cultural nationalists who treat religion as culture, such as the RSS, rely on inclusive cultural framing, and no source supports punishment.

women-must-cover.rationale: Dress mandates are not part of cultural nationalism in general; they depend on the religious setting.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union is not addressed in the sources, and the SEP notes cultural nations need not be states.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Herder defined peoples by language and culture and respected each, but pan-nationalist union is not stated.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The SEP says cultural nationalism can justify institutions that protect and develop the culture without a state of the group's own, such as self-governing cultural institutions within a federation.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The Zionist-versus-Bundist-style choice is not addressed in the general sources on cultural nationalism.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Cultural nationalism sees ideas, historical myth and culture as drivers of national renewal, in contrast to materialist accounts.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy is not addressed by cultural nationalism.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bank rescue policy is outside the doctrine.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Not addressed, though the SEP's liberal nationalists are friendly to constitutional limits.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Gender quotas are not addressed in the sources.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Not addressed; autarky is an economic-nationalist rather than cultural-nationalist idea.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Standards in trade deals are not addressed by the doctrine.

moral-incentives.rationale: Moral versus material incentives is a socialist-planning debate absent from cultural-nationalist sources.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Foco theory is a revolutionary-strategy doctrine; cultural nationalism is described as working through culture and ideas.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Not addressed; cultural nationalists lived under varied regimes.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Hutchinson and Smith describe cultural nationalists using history and the study of the past to build national identity, and Fichte argues the national spirit must be formed through education.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Herder strongly opposed colonialism and holds that forcing uniformity serves domination, and the doctrine values each culture's own development.

patriotic-education.rationale: Fichte argues the national spirit is created by educating the young, and cultural nationalists use schooling and history to build identity, though not always with flag rituals.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Affirmative action is not addressed by the sources.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary reform ideas are not addressed in the sources.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Debates about capitalism's crises are not part of cultural nationalism.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Cultivating influence in former imperial territories is not addressed; Herder opposed imperialism but that is not the same question.

delink-world-market.rationale: Dependency-theory prescriptions are not addressed by cultural nationalism.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist claim with no counterpart in the sources.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Private discrimination rules are a libertarian question that cultural nationalism does not address.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Constitutional rights design is not addressed in the sources, though the liberal-nationalist strand in the SEP is friendly to constraints.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Not addressed, though cultural nationalists generally sympathise with peoples divided without consent.

elective-rulers.rationale: Herder favoured republican government, but the sources do not extend this to the whole family.

minority-veto.rationale: Not addressed directly; the doctrine seeks collective national decisions and Herder's federalism accepts majority rule within local units.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The right of resistance is not addressed in the sources used for this profile.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliamentary supremacy is not addressed; cultural nationalism arose under monarchies and republics alike.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics is outside the doctrine.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal use is outside the doctrine.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Aristocratic duty is not addressed in the cultural-nationalist sources.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Cultural nationalists are activists for national renewal, and Fichte's addresses urge active national education.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: This is a critical-theory claim; cultural nationalism takes culture seriously but the sources do not address mass culture's function.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian hegemony is not addressed by the cultural-nationalism sources, though critics such as Calhoun and Hobsbawm stress elites' role in nation-making.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: World-systems theory is not addressed by the cultural-nationalism sources.

native-born-offices.rationale: Not addressed; a cultural definition of membership would not require native birth.

party-own-road.rationale: An intra-communist question that cultural nationalism does not address.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Development strategy is not discussed in the sources.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism is not stated as part of cultural nationalism; the SEP separates the cultural nation from the state.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Indigenous political leadership is not addressed in the sources.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Constitutional founding values are not addressed by the sources.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The equivalence debate is not addressed by the sources.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A historical dispute not addressed by the sources.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Preserving inherited symbols follows from the aim of sustaining national memory, but the sources do not address contested monuments.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Gender-policy attention is not addressed by cultural nationalism.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic violence policy is outside the doctrine.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Herder held that peoples differ deeply in values and that forced uniformity serves domination, so institutions should grow from each culture.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Cultural nationalism is a civil-society movement and Herder opposed militarism; no source supports a political army.

paid-care-work.rationale: Care-work recognition is not addressed in the sources.

filial-duty.rationale: Not addressed; traditional-minded strands would agree but the sources are silent.

office-by-exam.rationale: Civil-service recruitment is not addressed by the sources.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Economic-nationalist strands support this, but the cultural-nationalism sources do not address investment screening.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Divorce law is not addressed in the sources.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Imperative mandate is a radical-democratic idea absent from the sources.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is outside the doctrine.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Land tenure is not addressed by the sources.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Budgetary powers are not addressed by the sources.

single-official-language.rationale: Language is the core of national identity, so cultural nationalists tend to favour a common national language in schooling and public life, though Herder respected all peoples' languages.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Land-ownership limits are not discussed in the sources, though a protective cultural stance might sympathise.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Anti-discrimination legal doctrine is not addressed by the sources.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Romantic cultural nationalists sometimes criticised materialism, but the sources do not state it.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Covert warfare policy is not addressed by the doctrine.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: The Brezhnev-doctrine-style question is not addressed by cultural nationalism.

corporate-influence.rationale: Lobbying is not addressed in the sources.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Not addressed; a culture-protecting stance might favour it but the sources are silent.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Birth-rate policy is not stated in the sources, though some nationalist movements worry about demographics.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local property limits are not addressed in the sources.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employment policy is not addressed in the sources.

democratic-peace.rationale: Herder believed republics and wide participation would reduce war, but he did not state the democratic-peace claim.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Political obligation is not addressed in the cultural-nationalist sources.

non-intervention.rationale: Herder opposed imperial domination, which points toward non-interference, but no stated position exists.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is not addressed by the doctrine.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The conspiracy view belongs to ethnic and extremist nationalism; cultural nationalists as described include minorities who share the culture, as the RSS says of Muslims and Christians.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage law is not addressed in the sources.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Freedom-of-information law is not addressed by the sources.

local-production.rationale: Localism in production is an economic and green idea, not part of cultural nationalism as described.

informal-organisation.rationale: Affinity-group organisation is an anarchist idea; cultural nationalists work through cultural societies and schools.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Not addressed directly; self-determination is stressed but no position on international law follows.

religious-nation.rationale: Some cultural nationalisms define the nation by religion and many do not, as in Herder's language-based nation.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Cultural nationalism asserts each nation's own self-determination, which does not fit ritual submission to a power.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Fiscal federalism is not addressed in the sources.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: A distinction made in communist theory, not addressed by the sources.

defeat-communism.rationale: Cold War strategy is not addressed in the sources on cultural nationalism.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Public-service delivery models are not addressed.

religion-illusion.rationale: Cultural nationalists often treat religion as part of national culture, and Hutchinson notes the movements arose to replace challenged traditional religion with new cultural myths, so they do not call religion an illusion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: A Marxist historical claim not addressed by the sources.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: A socialist-feminist claim not addressed by the sources.

socialized-care.rationale: Public provision of housework is not addressed in the sources.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Fichte feared foreign influence on German, but Herder welcomed linguistic exchange, so adherents are split.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaty rights of nations within a state are not addressed in the sources, though cultural groups' claims to autonomy are discussed in general.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Herder favoured loosely federated local government, but not as cooperative property-holding communities.

majority-settlement.rationale: Not addressed; the cultural-nationalist stress on cultural rather than ethnic membership and Herder's respect for all nations point against it.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: A third-position economic claim that is not part of cultural nationalism, which has no economic programme in the sources.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Attachment to a historic homeland is central to national memory, but the sources do not rank claims.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not part of cultural nationalism, which as described in the sources has no such claim and rests on respect for the culture and history of peoples.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Sexual law is not addressed by the sources, and adherents differ by wider conservatism.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Herder favoured participation and Fichte values freedom as the soil of culture, so suppression is not part of it.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Blasphemy law is not addressed; it depends on whether religion forms part of the national culture.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Herder strongly opposed colonialism and imperialism.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: An Islamic legal claim outside cultural nationalism as described.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: An Islamist claim outside cultural nationalism as described.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Herder favoured broad participation but the doctrine does not specify it.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Intersectional analysis is not addressed in the sources.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Legal recognition of gender identity is not addressed in the sources.

assisted-dying.rationale: End-of-life law is outside the doctrine.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Cultural nationalism appears across the spectrum, but the sources do not take a view on the left-right division.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept not addressed in the sources.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Cultural nationalism as such does not hold this; the RSS example claims an inclusive cultural definition, though some strands are hostile.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Not addressed; religious-nationalist strands differ from Herder's secular reading of texts.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Religious dress rules are not addressed; they depend on the religion's place in the national culture.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Employment-law reforms are not addressed in the sources.

social-market-economy.rationale: Economic-order questions are not addressed by the sources.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Herder condemned war, but cultural nationalism does not call for abolishing defence, and many movements seek a state with armed forces.

rich-first.rationale: A development-strategy slogan not addressed by the sources.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Neutrality is not addressed in the sources.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Succession in office is not addressed by the sources.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: A mutualist idea not addressed by the sources.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: IMF conditionality is not addressed by the sources.

property-franchise.rationale: Cultural nationalists seek to build a community of the whole people around shared culture, and Herder favoured wide participation.

domination-women-nature.rationale: An ecofeminist claim not addressed by the sources.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept not addressed by the sources.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: A Marxist critique of press freedom not addressed in the sources.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Rule-of-law doctrine is not addressed in the sources.

racial-franchise.rationale: Herder rejected race and cultural nationalism defines the nation by culture, so a racial franchise contradicts it.

online-participation.rationale: E-democracy is not addressed in the sources.

open-government-data.rationale: Open-data policy is not addressed in the sources.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Not addressed; some Hindutva-linked activists support it, others do not.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a minority is an ethnic-nationalist practice, not cultural nationalism, and the SEP stresses inclusive identity.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Sortition assemblies are not addressed in the sources.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Herder interpreted sacred texts by secular means, but other strands treat tradition as fixed.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: A republican-egalitarian claim not addressed by the sources.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Military personnel policy on sexuality is not addressed in the sources.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Cultural nationalism builds identity on inherited culture, which often includes religion, and does not use the state to promote atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Cultural nationalists seek national institutions and the sources never support abolishing policing.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The SEP discusses devolution and federalism for cultural minorities, but power-sharing is not stated.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The relative merit of charity and welfare is not addressed in the sources.

term-limits.rationale: Term limits are not addressed in the sources.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid democracy is not addressed in the sources.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Extinction risk is not addressed in the sources.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Religious office eligibility is not addressed in the sources.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Marital authority is not addressed in the sources.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Not addressed; liberal and exclusive strands differ.

rent-control.rationale: Rent regulation is not addressed in the sources.

abolish-ip.rationale: Intellectual property is not addressed in the cultural-nationalist sources; adherents divide by wider economics, though they value authors and artists.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Fichte wanted national education of the young and Herder was hostile to militarism, but neither proposed drilled uniformed movements; inferred from their stress on education and cultural development.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear basing is a security question outside a doctrine about cultural community; the sources give no position.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Cultural nationalism does not require a sovereign state, and the sources say nothing on foreign bases, so adherents split.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Inferred from the doctrine's concern with a people's memory and history; no source discusses formal recognition of genocide.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Cultural nationalism has no economic programme in the sources; adherents range across the economic spectrum.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Herder opposed war and militarism, but nothing in the sources suggests absolute pacifism; inferred that adherents accept defence of persons and the nation.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Hutchinson's cultural nationalists revive an ancient golden age and Fichte treats language as continuous from the nation's origins; inferred rather than stated as a doctrine, and moderate strands stress cultural evolution.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Gender theory is outside the doctrine and the sources are silent; adherents split along wider cultural lines.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: A question of feminist theory that cultural nationalism never addresses.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Cultural nationalists cultivate national heroes and historical myth, so honouring those who died for the nation is likely, but 'martyrs and saints' is not stated in the sources and Herder disliked militarism.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Fichte speaks of national spirit, but no source frames politics as a struggle of good against evil; adherents are split.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Because the cultural nation need not be gathered in one state and can be sustained through institutions, a homeland serving as a cultural centre for a diaspora fits; inferred from the SEP's account, not stated for diasporas.

culture-before-state.rationale: Hutchinson's cultural nationalists aim at moral and cultural renewal, and Fichte treats the state as secondary to the nation and its education, so cultural renewal comes first.

god-not-male.rationale: Religious language is outside the doctrine; adherents vary with their religious traditions.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed by cultural nationalism; adherents' views depend on their religion.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Economic nationalism is excluded from this strand, and liberal cultural nationalists accept minority cultural rights; inferred from that.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Cultural nationalism can be pursued through autonomous institutions without redrawing administrative units; the sources give no position.

independent-unions.rationale: Cultural nationalism is about language and culture; it has no doctrine on unions, so adherents divide by wider economics.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The doctrine has no economic programme and does not define socialism, so adherents split by their wider politics.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Ownership of local services is outside a doctrine about cultural community; adherents follow ordinary left-right views.

second-chamber.rationale: Cultural nationalism does not require a particular legislature and may work within any polity, so this is neutral.

municipal-property.rationale: The doctrine has no programme on who owns productive assets; the sources treat it as compatible with different economies.

confederal-coordination.rationale: It seeks protection of the cultural nation, possibly through autonomous institutions, but does not prescribe confederal municipal structures.

family-wage.rationale: Wage levels are outside the doctrine, and the sources give no position.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Medical regulation is unrelated to cultural nationalism, so this is neutral.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Science funding for ageing is not addressed by the doctrine; adherents divide by wider views.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Financial privacy is outside the doctrine, which gives no position.

online-anonymity.rationale: Online anonymity is anachronistic and unrelated to the doctrine's concern with culture and language, so adherents split.

person-over-state.rationale: Herder stressed the individual's embeddedness in a people while Fichte put the nation above the state; the doctrine gives no firm view on person versus collective.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Inferred from Herder's and Fichte's view of language and culture as carriers of a people's spirit and memory, which implies politics should serve more than material needs.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The doctrine does not require a separate state and accepts autonomous cultural institutions, but sources say nothing on whether regional powers are entrenched.

gm-crops.rationale: Agricultural technology is unrelated to the doctrine, so adherents split.

dense-cities.rationale: Urban form is not addressed; the doctrine concerns culture, not environmental planning.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Cultural nationalism defines the nation by shared language, history and way of life rather than race, and Herder rejected ranking or organising peoples by race, so organising by race is outside it.

racial-pride.rationale: Inferred from the doctrine's focus on cultural rather than racial or ethnic descent; pride attaches to a shared culture and language, not to race or ancestry.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Inferred from Herder's criticism of conquest and empire in favour of plural peoples each developing their own culture.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Herder and Fichte define the nation by its shared language and history, and cultural nationalism does not require a common state or religion.

communal-electorates.rationale: Inferred: separate religious electorates would divide a nation defined by common culture, which cultural nationalists work to unite; the sources do not discuss them.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The sources do not treat foreign partition plots as part of the doctrine; adherents differ with their national situation.

free-public-college.rationale: Cultural nationalism prizes education as a vehicle of national culture but has no stated position on tuition; adherents divide on ordinary left-right lines.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Outside the doctrine; the sources give no environmental or tax position.

future-generations.rationale: Inferred from the view of the nation as a living cultural community carrying its memory across generations; the sources do not address the environment.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Outside the doctrine; the sources give no position on gender and public life.

arms-reduction.rationale: Outside the doctrine; cultural nationalism has no defence or arms programme of its own.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Outside the doctrine; the sources do not discuss diplomatic procedure.

capital-controls.rationale: Cultural nationalism has no economic programme of its own, so adherents divide on capital controls.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Cultural nationalism is about language and culture, not the monopoly of force, and the sources do not discuss it; adherents split along ordinary lines.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred: Fichte's Addresses call on the young to defend the nation and Herder's pacifism is directed at empire, so a duty to refuse war between states is not a cultural-nationalist position.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The doctrine has no economic programme, so adherents divide along ordinary left-right lines on labour relations.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: The doctrine has no economic programme and the sources never discuss wage supplements.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Fiscal policy lies outside a movement centred on culture and language.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The sources do not treat the international economic order; cultural nationalists include both anticolonial and conservative strands.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Inferred: cultural nationalism works through education and institutions and does not require a separate state, so it favours reform or autonomy within existing structures over smashing the state.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Economic pluralism is not addressed by the doctrine, which has no economic programme.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Environmental valuation is not addressed in the sources; adherents divide along ordinary lines.

sacred-nation.rationale: Cultural nationalists such as Herder and Fichte treat the nation as a living, enduring spiritual community that gives individuals meaning through shared language and memory, though not always in religious terms.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student finance is not addressed; this is a general economic question on which adherents split.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Cultural nationalists sometimes claim a dominant culture suppresses minority cultures within a state, but the economic exploitation claim is not part of the doctrine.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Herder stresses the diversity of national cultures and Fichte stresses national particularity, so a fixed shared human nature is not central; the sources do not settle it.

public-service-media.rationale: Inferred: cultural nationalists promote public cultural and educational institutions that sustain a national language, which public broadcasters often serve, but independence from government is not discussed.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Herder held that each people's culture and religion is distinct and valuable, so a typical cultural nationalist sees religions as plural expressions of peoples rather than one truth; inferred, as the sources do not address the claim directly.

farm-price-support.rationale: Cultural nationalism has no economic programme, so farm support is not addressed and adherents split by their wider economics.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Nuclear policy is outside a doctrine about cultural community, and the sources give no position.

workers-own-party.rationale: Class politics is outside cultural nationalism, which stresses the whole cultural nation, so adherents have no common line.

ban-fgm.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; inferred from liberal cultural nationalism's commitment to individual rights within a national culture, though some adherents defend custom.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; inferred from the moderate and liberal strands (Gans, Tamir), which accept equal individual rights, while the doctrine itself is silent.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Fichte and Herder treat a shared language as the basis of one nation, so a language spoken across regions counts as one; inferred, since the sources do not discuss regional naming disputes.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Pollution liability is outside the doctrine and the sources give no position, so adherents split by wider economics.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Cultural nationalists value tradition but the sources say nothing on chiefs in lawmaking, and liberal strands favour elected bodies; adherents are split.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Environmental policy is outside the doctrine and the sources give no position, so adherents split by wider ideology.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Criminal sentencing is outside a doctrine about culture, and the sources give no position.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Language is central to cultural nationalism and Fichte and Gans stress it as the carrier of national culture, so adherents would back a language requirement; inferred, as the sources do not state it for immigrants, and liberal nationalists accept integration demands.

missingStatements.text: A nation should be defined by its shared language, history and culture rather than by descent or political citizenship.
missingStatements.rationale: Defining nationhood culturally, with language at the centre, is the core claim attributed to Herder and Fichte and to cultural nationalism generally.

missingStatements.text: The state should support its national language, literature, arts and folk traditions.
missingStatements.rationale: Cultural nationalists work to sustain and develop the national culture, and the SEP says this can justify institutions that protect and develop it.

missingStatements.text: Writers, scholars and artists have a leading role in forming a nation's identity.
missingStatements.rationale: Hutchinson and Smith describe intellectuals as central creators of national character and historical myth, and Herder collected popular songs to this end.
missingStatements.declined: Role of intellectuals in forming national identity is a scholarly claim, not a contested political question.

notes: Strands differ: Fichte is more statist and wary of foreign influence, Herder more pluralist and cosmopolitan, and Hindutva-linked cultural nationalism adds religious positions that the general profile leaves at 0.
